paper.title: Scalable Unitary State-Encoding for Generic Large Data
paper.abstract: Efficient encoding of data into quantum states remains a fundamental bottleneck in many quantum computing protocols, which would otherwise offer advantages over their classical counterparts. Here, we introduce deterministic and scalable amplitude-encoding methods with low two-qubit gate costs and tunable trade-offs between circuit depth and encoding fidelity. Our approaches require no amplitude amplification or mid-circuit measurement and are capable of encoding arbitrary complex data or queryable functions by using tensor-networks to go beyond what can be held in classical memory. Our principle contributions are two complementary algorithms for simplifying fully controlled multiplexer circuits to one- and two-qubit gates. In the first, we formally map the elimination of redundant gate controls to a Boolean logic minimization problem, while in the second we utilize a single ancilla qubit to map the multi-controlled rotation gates to a sequence of one- and two-qubit operations via the Walsh-Hadamard spectrum of the gate angles. We benchmark these methods across a broad range of function classes, characterizing their total depth in an all-to-all connectivity graph against system size and target fidelity. Hybridizing our methods gives up to orders of magnitude improvement in circuit depth at equivalent state fidelity compared to the default state-preparation method in the Qiskit package. We furthermore demonstrate our method on IQM hardware with a square lattice connectivity, finding excellent fidelity, even with minimal noise mitigation. By significantly reducing gate depth for encoding, this work enables the experimental execution of applications on current and near-term hardware which would otherwise be reduced to noise before the first calculation step, shortening the time horizon to robust quantum utility.

paper.title: Quantum subsets discrimination and key sifting with success probability one
paper.abstract: Non-distinguishability of non-orthogonal quantum states is the essential feature of quantum mechanics. In particular, one cannot deterministically orthogonalize the set of quantum states, while probabilistic orthogonalization is possible, including unambiguous state discrimination and discrimination between the subsets. Here, we propose a method for error-free subsets discrimination with significantly increased success probability, which may reach one even for non-orthogonal and linearly dependent input states. This method may be applied in quantum cryptography: An alternative basis reconciliation procedure is described, which may provide unit sifting probability even for a large number of bases and for non-orthogonal states within each basis.

paper.title: Magic Can Superactivate Quantum Capacity
paper.abstract: Environmental magic can enable two channels with zero quantum capacity to transmit quantum information jointly. We establish this superactivation within a family of discrete quantum convolution channels with fixed Clifford interactions. For the couplings considered, stabilizer-mixture environments induce entanglement-breaking channels. We construct a mixed magic environment whose induced channel has positive private capacity and a Choi state with positive partial transpose, hence zero quantum capacity. A half-erasure auxiliary activates this channel through the Smith--Yard mechanism. Finite-block encoding and decoding over a self-complementary convolution auxiliary then realize a higher-dimensional erasure channel that still permits activation. We also bound the activated capacity by the modified relative entropy of magic of the main environment. Replacing either environment of the convolution pair by any stabilizer mixture makes the joint quantum capacity vanish, identifying environmental magic as a necessary resource on both sides for this realization.

paper.title: Twisted Compactification, Quotient Quantum Codes and Logical Gates
paper.abstract: Many quantum codes, including balanced-product, bivariate-bicycle and genon codes and the five-qubit code, are quotient codes: a larger code folded onto itself by identifying each check with its image under a deck transformation composed with a symmetry. We show that this is the lattice form of twisted compactification, in which a theory on $X\times F$ carries a symmetry background along $F$, and we use the correspondence in both directions. For monomial quotients of Pauli stabilizer codes, a transfer theorem gives the logical qudits, logical operators and distance bounds from those of the parent, with a Tate cohomology group counting the logical operators that are new. For higher-form and cup-product symmetries the twist is an entangling diagonal circuit; when a finite cover trivializes the background, the code is a dressed quotient, so abelian Pauli codes give non-abelian topological order such as $D(D_4)$. The dressings have Clifford level at most one less than the degree of the twist, and for cubic twists the code dimension is a count of solutions of quadratic equations in cup products, which certifies that the code is not a Pauli stabilizer code when it is not a power of two; on tori and slabs the distance is linear in the size. Twists also create logical gates: three toric codes on $S^3$ have no logical qubits, but on $\mathbb{RP}^3$ the same circuit is a logical $CCZ$. A quarter-turn twist of the 3D fermionic toric code gives codes of linear distance, from $[[768,2,9]]$ up, whose $p+ip$ pump is an explicit finite-time quasi-local evolution that preserves the code space exactly; using the spin-topological response formula of Barkeshli, Hsin and Kobayashi, we identify its logical action as $T$ up to Clifford factors. Finally, twisting abelian gauge theories reach only the quantum doubles $D(G)$ with $[G,G]$ central.

paper.title: Tomography of approximately Gaussian mixed states
paper.abstract: Moment-based tomography efficiently reconstructs Gaussian states, but stochastic phase noise generally produces mixed, non-Gaussian outputs. For approximately Gaussian outputs, we formulate reconstruction as a problem in quantum learning theory under model misspecification. Our trace-distance guarantee separates the intrinsic Gaussian approximation error from statistical errors in estimating the first moments and covariance matrix. Using recent Gaussian trace-distance bounds, we obtain linear dependence of the statistical contribution on moment errors when the covariance inverses remain bounded, improving on the square-root dependence on covariance error in earlier guarantees. A Fock-space truncation procedure provides certified, convergent lower and upper bounds on the intrinsic error. Under an explicit sub-Gaussian condition on the heterodyne outcomes, the sufficient sample count scales inversely with the square of the allowed statistical error remaining after accounting for the approximation error. We verify the statistical condition for stochastic phase rotations and heralded unitary-averaged states with bounded input squeezing. We apply the framework to probabilistic unitary averaging for phase noise reduction, quantifying reconstruction error and accounting for heralding overhead in the total number of estimation attempts.

paper.title: Parametric $\mathrm{CZ}$ Gates in a Tunable Tripod Architecture with Fixed-Frequency Superconducting Qubits
paper.abstract: Efficient implementation of the operations required for quantum error correction in superconducting quantum computers requires high gate fidelity, adequate qubit connectivity, and selective control of interactions. Sharing a single coupler among multiple qubits can improve connectivity, but also requires accounting for its effects on qubits outside the target pair. In this work, we numerically investigate the feasibility of implementing parametric-resonance $\mathrm{CZ}$ gates in a tunable tripod structure consisting of three fixed-frequency transmon qubits connected to a single tunable coupler. We modulate the external flux applied to the coupler and optimize the pulse parameters for each qubit pair to construct $\mathrm{CZ}_{01}$, $\mathrm{CZ}_{02}$, and $\mathrm{CZ}_{12}$ gates. We calculate the time evolution of a Hamiltonian that includes three energy levels for each circuit element and evaluate gate fidelity and leakage after virtual Z correction. The fidelities obtained for the target-pair computational blocks, whose input and output basis states have both the coupler and spectator qubit in their ground states, are 0.9943, 0.9834, and 0.9907, respectively. We also find that population preservation at the end of the gate depends on the initial state of the spectator qubit. These results demonstrate the possibility of constructing $\mathrm{CZ}$ operations for each qubit pair through flux modulation of a shared coupler while maintaining fixed data-qubit frequencies. They also highlight the need to evaluate performance and optimize control over the full computational space, including the spectator qubit.

paper.title: From spectroscopy to quantum dynamics: assessing reduced models of a NaCs molecular gate
paper.abstract: We investigate how spectroscopic calibration and basis selection affect predictions for a dipolar-exchange gate between two optically trapped $^{23}$Na$^{133}$Cs molecules. We construct a 128-state molecular Hamiltonian restricted to the $N=0,1$ rotational manifold, fit two effective optical parameters to three bright microwave transitions, and compare the resulting spectrum with four additional lines. In the coherent pair model, changing the optical polarization angle by $+0.1^\circ$ reduces the calculated gate fidelity from 94.64\% to 1.09\% at fixed carrier frequencies. Retuning the carriers and restoring the target Rabi frequencies recovers 89.31\%. The remaining sensitivity reflects changes in the multilevel pair dynamics that are not removed by target-frequency and target-Rabi recalibration. Enlarging the molecular basis produces nonmonotonic changes in fidelity, although the 11-state and 25-state calculations give closely agreeing logical maps after phase alignment. Two controls with isolated transfer probabilities near 98.45\% yield complete-gate fidelities differing by more than 11 percentage points. We relate these comparisons to a sufficient bound on the error of a projected propagator. The numerical tests quantify agreement among selected bases for a specified coherent Hamiltonian.

paper.title: Features of Non-Local Quantum Correlations in Nuclei
paper.abstract: Classical simulation of quantum many-body systems is challenged by the combined effects of entanglement and non-stabilizerness (magic). Non-local magic, $M^{\mathrm{NL}}_α$, quantifies the component of non-stabilizerness that cannot be removed by local unitary transformations and provides a measure of quantum complexity beyond entanglement alone. It is bounded from below by the antiflatness of the entanglement spectrum, ${F}_A$. We calculate stabilizer Rényi entropies, non-local magic, entanglement-spectrum antiflatness, and entanglement entropy in shell-model ground states of more than 260 even-even, odd-even, and odd-odd nuclei, using a bipartition into proton and neutron sectors. We find that the previously established bound $4{F}_A\leq{M}^{\mathrm{NL}}_{\mathrm{lin}}$ holds for every nucleus studied and approaches saturation in the limit of separable states. Odd-odd nuclei exhibit markedly different patterns of entanglement and magic compared with even-even and odd-even systems, revealing distinctive signatures of proton-neutron quantum correlations and providing new insight into the complexity generated by nuclear interactions.

paper.title: Random encoders and expurgation improve 1,873 entries of the Grassl qubit code tables
paper.abstract: I report 192 explicit binary stabilizer codes $[[n,k,d]]$ with $53\le n\le 254$ and $5\le d\le 13$ whose minimum distance exceeds the lower bound listed in Grassl's code tables at the same $(n,k)$: 161 codes by one and 31 by two. Through the standard propagation rules they raise 1,873 entries of the table. For 190 of the codes, a random Clifford encoder is followed by expurgation: every logical operator of weight below the target distance is enumerated, and a few logical operators are promoted to stabilizers so that each low-weight one anticommutes with at least one of them. The other two are obtained by puncturing a code from the table and repairing it in the same way. All 192 distances are exact: the lower bound is certified by exhaustive meet-in-the-middle enumeration of up to $4\times10^{13}$ Pauli operators, and the upper bound by an explicit logical operator of weight $d$. A first-moment count explains the results. Expurgated random codes have about eight more logical qubits than a typical random code of the same length and distance, so they beat the table wherever its best known codes are no better than random. The largest gains, up to nine logical qubits, are at $d\ge9$ and $n\gtrsim170$, where the table often gives a lower bound without an explicit code. The same count predicts improvements at 619 further pairs $(n,d)$. The search was run by AI agents. The codes, their certificates and an independent checker are public.

paper.title: What are local complementations, really?
paper.abstract: A local complementation at a vertex $v$ of a graph $G$ replaces the induced neighborhood of $v$ with its complement. Local complementations are, at face value, peculiar operations. Yet they famously show up when describing the local Clifford equivalence among graph states, and, because of this, have become a fundamental notion in the study of graph states. Following Bouchet, we show here how local complementations on graphs are more naturally thought of in terms of switchings of (matroid) bases of stabilizer states. Bases and switchings reveal structural properties of stabilizer states that are harder to glean from the graph-theoretic description alone, such as vertex-minors and statistics of local Pauli measurements. Bases also simplify prior proofs about graphs up to local complementations, of which we give several examples. Bases are foundational in the study of (multi)matroids; as such this paper serves as a gentle introduction to the applications of multimatroids to quantum information theory.

paper.title: Magic Is in the Eye of the Measure
paper.abstract: Magic, or nonstabilizerness, is the quantum resource behind universal quantum computation. Its applications in high-energy and nuclear physics rely almost exclusively on the stabilizer Rényi entropy (SRE), although magic has no unique measure. For two qubits, we compare the SRE with three measures defined through optimizations over stabilizer states: the min- and max-relative entropies of magic and the logarithmic free robustness. We determine the maximal-magic states of all four measures, with exact proofs, and find that they depend on the measure. In the determination of the weak mixing angle from minimal magic in Møller scattering, the min-relative entropy gives an energy-dependent value that differs from that of the SRE, whereas the max-relative entropy and the logarithmic free robustness give $\sin^2θ_W=1/4$ at all energies. We trace this difference to the non-analytic structure of the optimization-based measures. Physical conclusions drawn from extremizing magic can thus depend on the measure.

paper.title: Conveyor-mode electron shuttling through a T-junction in Si/SiGe
paper.abstract: Conveyor-mode shuttling in gated Si/SiGe devices enables adiabatic transfer of single electrons, electron patterns and spin qubits confined in quantum dots across several microns with a scalable number of signal lines. To realize their full potential, linear shuttle lanes must connect into a two-dimensional grid with controllable routing. We introduce a T-junction device linking two independently driven shuttle lanes. Electron routing across the junction requires no extra control lines beyond the four channels per conveyor belt. We measure an inter-lane charge transfer fidelity of $$F={100.0000000}_{-9\times 1{0}^{-7}}^{+0}\,\%$$ F = 100.0000000 − 9 × 1 0 − 7 + 0 % at an instantaneous electron velocity of 270 mm s −1 . The filling of 54 quantum dots is controlled by simple atomic pulses, allowing us to swap electron patterns, laying the groundwork for a native spin-qubit SWAP gate. This T-junction establishes a path towards scalable, two-dimensional quantum computing architectures with flexible spin qubit routing for quantum error correction.

paper.title: Plotkin-optimal pure quantum LRCs with large minimum distances from NMDS codes
paper.abstract: Quantum locally recoverable codes (qLRCs) are a class of quantum error-correcting codes that can recover an erased qudit by accessing only a few other qudits. This paper develops a general framework for constructing optimal pure qLRCs that attain the Plotkin-like bound, referred to as Plotkin-optimal pure qLRCs, from Hermitian dual-containing near maximum-distance separable (NMDS) codes. Focusing on a special class of NMDS codes called extended subcodes of generalized Reed-Solomon (ESGRS) codes, we determine their localities by analyzing certain subset sum problems over finite fields. By further exploiting the algebraic structures of ESGRS codes and related codes, we construct four families of Plotkin-optimal pure qLRCs with large lengths and more flexible minimum distances than existing constructions. These constructions provide strong global error-correction capability while retaining local recovery. To the best of our knowledge, they give the first families of qLRCs attaining the pure Plotkin-like bound. In addition, by using the resulting locality property, we resolve in the negative a related problem on ESGRS codes supporting combinatorial designs.

paper.title: Long-lived quantum memories with rare-earth ions doped in crystals
paper.abstract: Quantum memory is a core enabling device for large-scale quantum networks, serving as the fundamental building block for quantum repeaters and transportable quantum memories. Among various physical platforms, rare-earth-ion-doped crystals stand out as one of the most promising solid-state candidates for long-lived photonic quantum memories, owing to their exceptionally long spin coherence time and their compatibility with integration. In this review, we first introduce the physical mechanisms underlying long-lived spin coherence in rare-earth systems, with particular emphasis on the zero-first-order-Zeeman transition and dynamical decoupling techniques. We then review the experimental progress in this field, highlighting three distinct lifetimes--the spin coherence time, the light storage time, and the quantum storage time--and covering experiments that have achieved hour-scale spin coherence, minute- to hour-scale light storage, and minute-scale single-photon-level quantum storage. Finally, we discuss the remaining challenges that hinder the realization of practical long-lived quantum memories, explore potential strategies to overcome these obstacles, and outline the prospects for their future applications in quantum networks.

paper.title: Stabilizer Learning under Global Depolarizing Noise with Polynomial Copies and $2^t$ Time
paper.abstract: We study learning the stabilizer structure of an unknown pure $n$-qubit state observed through global depolarizing noise of unknown strength, with a fixed promised upper bound below one, using destructive two-copy Bell measurements. Let $0\le t\le n$ bound the stabilizer nullity, let $\varepsilon>0$ be the accuracy, and let $0<δ<1$ be the failure tolerance. With probability at least $1-δ$, a learner must return a commuting unsigned Pauli group containing every stabilizer of the pure state; averaging conjugation by that group must decrease the purity of the observed noisy state by at most $\varepsilon$. Tang and Steckmann gave such a learner with polynomially many copies and $2^t$ times polynomial time when the noise strength is below a threshold of at most about $0.16$, which tends to zero as $t/n\to1$. They asked whether other algorithms with these resources can exceed this threshold. We answer this question affirmatively for every fixed bound on global depolarizing noise below one and every $0\le t\le n$, including states with only one promised independent stabilizer. Our learner uses polynomially many copies and $2^t$ times polynomial classical running time. All resource bounds hold on every execution. Their polynomial factors depend on $n,1/\varepsilon,\log(1/δ)$, with degrees and constants depending on the fixed noise promise.

paper.title: Logical-Class Diagnostic Layer for Stabilizer Codes and Decoders via Supercharge Structures
paper.abstract: We develop a decoder-agnostic logical-class diagnostic layer for abelian Pauli stabilizer codes, motivated by fault-tolerant quantum computing. An ancilla fermionic register defines a nilpotent supercharge whose clean degree-zero harmonic sector is the code space. Projected-return blocks derived from graded commutators organize the recovery test of whether a decoder-selected correction preserves every encoded input for every error in a declared same-syndrome family; the passing syndromes form the certified faithful window. Demoting the supercharge to an exact binary diagnostic formulation classifies residuals modulo stabilizers, separating a check violation, a harmless stabilizer residual, and a syndrome-silent nontrivial logical action, with a two-sector form for CSS codes. Because the unknown fault cancels, the relative logical class of two record-compatible candidates is computable online. We verify the diagnostic formalisms on the Steane code and specify a static--circuit bridge audit protocol for the Gross bivariate-bicycle quantum low-density parity-check (qLDPC) code. The method supplements existing decoders without additional physical qubits for software use.

paper.title: Floquet engineering of quantum relaxation
paper.abstract: Dynamical decoupling suppresses decoherence by averaging selected interactions between a quantum system and its environment. Here, we extend this notion through a general Floquet formalism that maps periodic control onto relaxation and dephasing channels. Environmental fluctuations are decomposed into Floquet components that sample the noise spectrum at distinct frequencies, with coupling strengths determined by control-induced Floquet coefficients. We experimentally investigate this approach using a single nitrogen-vacancy center in diamond under multi-pulse control. By tuning the drive and detuning, we reshape the coupling to environmental fluctuations and create isolated operating points where the dominant decoherence channel vanishes, strongly suppressing Floquet dephasing. The resulting coherence enhancement follows the predicted Floquet coupling coefficients and can be shifted by modifying the control sequence. These results establish Floquet driving as a general framework for engineering transverse and longitudinal relaxation through the design of quantum control protocols.

paper.title: All-to-All Connectivity in Superconducting Qubits via Metamaterial-Mediated Interactions
paper.abstract: We show that encoding superconducting qubits as dual-rail or spin-locked transmons lets a metamaterial waveguide couple them all-to-all while suppressing the spurious entanglement that burdens shared-mode architectures, a step toward the non-local connectivity that quantum low-density parity-check codes require. In a bare-transmon architecture, the dispersive coupling between each populated mode and every idle qubit attached to it entangles spectators with the gate, and cancelling it by dynamical decoupling lengthens every gate. The encoding suppresses this coupling at the hardware level, from second to fourth order in the inverse qubit--mode detuning. A two-tone cross-resonance drive then generates a Mølmer-Sørensen interaction between encoded qubits, which we use for an entangling gate and a joint parity measurement, both selective and parallelizable through different modes. Simulating two dual-rail transmons sharing three resonators with a mode lifetime of $30\,μ$s, we find that heralding transmon relaxation as erasure leaves a gate infidelity of $1.4\times10^{-3}$ at $152$~ns, dominated by photon loss. Photon loss and mode crowding together bound the array size. The gate duration must exceed the inverse mode spacing, which shrinks as the array lengthens, while photon loss grows with gate duration. This bound grows linearly with the mode lifetime and with the inter-resonator coupling; at a lifetime of $150\,μ$s, five times the simulated value, and a coupling of $80$~MHz, a $10^{-3}$ error budget admits $13$ qubits on $25$ resonators.

paper.title: Normal Factor Graph Representations of Stabilizer Quantum Codes with Applications
paper.abstract: We develop normal factor graph (NFG) representations of stabilizer quantum error-correcting codes and entanglement-assisted quantum error-correcting codes. We introduce two complementary representations. Quantum-code NFGs describe stabilizer and normalizer label codes and provide a graphical framework for establishing self-orthogonality, constructing codes from component codes, and identifying encoding and decoding circuits. Quantum-probability NFGs represent the quantum-mechanical probabilities associated with encoding, noise, and measurement. We also introduce a doubleedge formulation that makes the relationship between these two representations explicit. We apply the framework to convolutional and tail-biting convolutional stabilizer codes, as well as to two classes of low-density parity-check stabilizer codes. Finally, we extend the quantum-probability representation to entanglementassisted codes.

paper.title: Binary Quantum Hypothesis Testing with a Rejection Option: The Exact Error-Exponent Trade-off
paper.abstract: We characterize the exact error-exponent trade-off in binary quantum hypothesis testing with a rejection option for faithful states on a finite-dimensional Hilbert space. The probabilities of rejection under the two hypotheses are required to vanish exponentially, with exponents at least $K$ and $L$. We show that a quadruple $(a,b,K,L)$ of positive error and rejection exponents is achievable if and only if it satisfies three single-letter conditions: two conditions involve Petz--Rényi quantities and coincide with the converse bound conjectured to be tight by Ji and Regula; the third involves the $α$--$z$ Rényi quantities on the triangle $\max\{α,1-α\}\le z\le1$. The proof combines a sector decomposition inside Schur--Weyl blocks, an explicit one-shot measurement construction, and an exact minimax argument.

paper.title: Multicopy teleportation and quantum program retrieval on superconducting quantum hardware
paper.abstract: Correction-free teleportation protocols offer a probabilistic route around the limits imposed by the quantum no-programming theorem, but have remained largely theoretical. Here, we experimentally implement and benchmark correction-free multicopy teleportation on noisy superconducting quantum hardware. Key to this is an efficient circuit implementation: by suitably decomposing the unitary that maps the multicopy measurement basis onto the computational basis, we substantially reduce circuit depth and gate count. For one- and two-qubit input states, using $k=2$ and $3$ copies, we observe success probabilities substantially exceeding the single-copy bound with fidelities above 0.85. We further explore applications to probabilistic programmable quantum processors, in particular the storage and retrieval of unitary operations encoded in quantum program states. Our results establish the practical feasibility of multicopy teleportation and highlight its potential for near-term quantum processors and distributed quantum computing.

paper.title: Quantum algorithm for weakly correlated molecular electronic ground states with sub-quintic scaling in the system size
paper.abstract: Weakly correlated electronic structures are predominant among molecules, and are routinely solved with heuristic classical methods such as the ``gold standard'' CCSD(T) coupled cluster model, incurring a formal time complexity $O(n^7)$ in the number of molecular orbitals and with no guarantee of energy error $\varepsilon$ at or below chemical accuracy. In this work, a quantum algorithm is presented for ground state energy estimation of weakly correlated molecules using Trotterized time evolution, with an end-to-end quantum operations cost that scales as $\tilde{O}(n^{4.8}/\varepsilon^2)$ in the limit of high-order product formulae when run as a low-depth, shot-noise limited algorithm, or $\tilde{O}(n^{4.8} + n^{3.8}/\varepsilon)$ when scaling the simulation time $T\propto 1/\varepsilon$. The algorithm combines adiabatic state preparation using a smoothed Gevrey schedule with eigenstate filtering via quantum prolate diagonalization (QPD). Both steps of the algorithm rely on a size-independent spectral gap assumption, which is validated by numerical studies on alanine chains with up to 64 monomers. We benchmark the performance of our eigenstate filtering algorithm on a set of 28 molecules to compare our approach against prior phase estimation algorithms, finding that QPD achieves state-of-the-art cost tradeoffs for $\varepsilon$-accurate results. Physical quantum resource estimates are obtained for running Trotter step circuits with up to 40 spin-orbitals, providing a clear path for scaling up quantum simulation of chemistry on early fault-tolerant hardware.

paper.title: The exact information cost of randomized measurements in quantum metrology
paper.abstract: Randomized measurements provide state-independent readout for multiparameter quantum sensing. Although 3-designs retain a constant fraction of the quantum Fisher information (QFI) for every pure state, we show that 2-designs need not. In dimension \(d\), complete mutually unbiased bases (MUBs) retain exactly \(1/(d+1)\) of the QFI in the worst state and direction, attaining the universal lower bound for 2-designs built from orthonormal bases; symmetric informationally complete (SIC) measurements retain exactly \((1-1/\sqrt{d+1})/d\). The loss comes from aligned blind spots. Relative to a basis, pure-state changes split into population and phase parts of equal dimension, but probabilities respond only to the former. Mutual unbiasedness turns a population change for one basis into a phase change for every other. The worst case already occurs for a qubit encoded in two levels. Independent random bases instead scatter their blind spots. In sufficiently large dimensions, five Haar-random bases retain, with high probability, a dimension-independent QFI fraction for every pure state and direction. Random Clifford measurements on any number of qubits retain exactly one third. Thus blind-spot geometry, not second-order symmetry alone, controls worst-case metrological performance.

paper.title: Optimal Estimation in Weak Value Amplification with a Position Pointer
paper.abstract: We experimentally evaluate five estimators for weak-value amplification (WVA) using a position pointer to measure birefringence time delays. Two general approaches are considered: measuring the position shift $Δx$ and measuring the probability change $ΔP_w$ of successful postselection. Specifically, five estimators are investigated: CCD-detected fringe shift $Δx$, quadrant photodiode (PDQ) transversal voltage difference (XDIFF), and lock-in amplifier output phase $η$ (for $Δx$ measurement), as well as PDQ total output voltage (SUM) and CCD-detected average photon number $N_r$ (for $ΔP_w$ measurement). The measurement precision is characterized by the Allan deviation over a range of input laser powers $P_0$. Generally, measuring the position shift $Δx$ yields higher precision than measuring the probability change $ΔP_w$. At $P_0=0.5$~mW, corresponding to a laser-power-limited regime, direct measurement of the fringe displacement with the CCD achieves a minimum Allan deviation of $(5.30\pm0.10)\times10^{-3}$~as, approaching the corresponding photon-statistical Cramér--Rao bound (CRB). At $P_0=50$~mW, corresponding to a detector-limited regime, PDQ detection combined with lock-in demodulation provides the best precision, reaching $(1.80\pm0.06)\times10^{-3}$~as and remaining close to the corresponding CRB. These results demonstrate that the optimal readout depends on the available optical power, detector dynamic range, and technical noise, providing practical guidance for selecting readout strategies in high-precision WVA-based metrology.

paper.title: Early Fault-Tolerant Magic State Synthesis and Spacetime Efficient Analog Rotations with Color Code on a Superconducting Quantum Processor
paper.abstract: With recent improvements to syndrome extraction scheduling and decoding, and the availability of complete transversal Clifford operations and lattice surgery, color code is an especially promising platform for quantum processors with local connectivity. The key ingredient for universal computation is thus generating useful magic states with limited resources. Space-Time Efficient Analog Rotations (STAR) and Fault-tolerant magic state synthesis (MSS) are two such methods for magic state generation, targeted for near-term and long-term quantum computing, respectively. In this work, we perform the first implementations of both magic state paradigms on a superconducting quantum processor. We present a STAR-type injection protocol on the color code, with favorable error rate and spacetime costs versus prior protocols on both the color and surface codes. We then implement a MSS factory by performing multi-patch magic state cultivations, interleaved with transversal Clifford operations, and lattice-surgery magic state teleportation. Under post-selection, we achieve a kickback tomography correct sign probability of $99.9859\%$ on cultivated $T_L$ states, $96\%$ tomographic fidelity on logical analog rotation states, and $91\%$ fidelity on synthesized logical magic states consuming 3 cultivated $T_L$ states, 3 transversal Hadamard operations, and real-time feed-forward $S_L$ corrections during magic state teleportation. We compare the efficacy of post-selection, Most-Likely-Error (MLE) decoding, and concatenated-matching decoding throughout, highlighting the potential of end-to-end color code computation.

paper.title: Resource efficient Sample Based Quantum Simulation through Fragmentation and Virtual Partitioning of QPU
paper.abstract: Present-day sample-based quantum algorithms within quantum-centric supercomputing workflows require substantial classical post-processing, large circuit depths to produce chemically relevant samples, and long QPU times to execute the many circuits needed for molecules of chemically relevant size. We introduce FMO-QVM-HCI-HSQD, a resource-efficient sample-based framework that breaks a large problem into fragments, runs the fragments in parallel on virtual regions of the QPU, and reduces circuit depth through a half-qubit ansatz whose samples seed an HCI expansion. We demonstrate the algorithm on ibm_marrakesh and ibm_boston for the water trimer and the carmofur_Mpro complex with up to 52 qubits, benchmarking against FMO-CCSD(T), FMO-CASCI and FMO-HCI. For the water trimer (14 spin orbitals for monomers, 28 for dimers), our method reduces the two-qubit depth by 39% compared to FMO-QVM-SQD and the QPU time by 82% compared to sequential FMO-SQD, and accesses 3% of the determinant subspace versus 40% for FMO-SQD, while achieving more accurate energies. For the carmofur_Mpro complex (16 and 32 spin orbitals), it reduces the two-qubit depth by 47% and the QPU time by 20% compared to FMO-QVM-SQD, and accesses 0.007% of the determinant subspace versus 40%, while remaining within chemical accuracy. Extending the carmofur_Mpro active space in the 6-31G basis to 52 and 104 spin orbitals, sampled on 26 and 52 qubits, the total energy deviates from FMO-HCI by only 1.22 mHa. These results show that combining fragmentation, virtual QPU partitioning and half-qubit sampling makes sample-based quantum simulation of chemically relevant systems feasible on current hardware.

paper.title: Statistical Foundations of Reinforcement Learning: A Non-Asymptotic Perspective
paper.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) embodies a foundational paradigm for sequential decision-making in the face of uncertainty. The rapid growth of model complexity in emerging applications has significantly amplified the challenges of achieving data-efficient RL, particularly in sample-starved scenarios where data collection may be costly, time-consuming, or even high-stakes. Consequently, understanding and improving the data efficiency of RL algorithms has become a central problem of both fundamental theoretical interest and practical importance. Despite decades of research, the statistical underpinnings of RL remained remarkably underdeveloped until relatively recently, particularly in the finite-sample regimes most relevant to modern practice. Over the past few years, there has been a surge of activity advancing the frontiers of non-asymptotic statistical RL theory, drawing on ideas from high-dimensional statistics and probability, information theory, and statistical learning theory. In this monograph, we present a non-asymptotic treatment for RL based on tabular Markov decision processes, focusing on three canonical sampling mechanisms --- RL with a generative model, online RL, and offline RL --- together with two algorithmic paradigms: model-based and model-free approaches. Centered around non-asymptotic sample complexity analysis, our treatment emphasizes minimax-optimal algorithm design, particularly methods that attain statistical optimality without significant burn-in costs, as well as sharp statistical characterizations of several widely used RL algorithms. Whenever possible, we provide largely self-contained analyses together with intuitive explanations. We also briefly discuss several extensions, such as robust RL, competitive multi-agent RL, federated RL, uncertainty quantification, and RL from human feedback.

paper.title: Engineered Learning Problems on Noisy Quantum Processors
paper.abstract: Despite quantum machine learning being an active topic of research, demonstrations of algorithms run on quantum hardware beating classical methods remain rare. In this work, we demonstrate a significant performance gap using a projected quantum kernel for $n=15,30$ and $45$ qubits over classical methods on an engineered classification problem, and show reproducibility of the results over different quantum processor units. We also demonstrate how error mitigation can widen this gap, both by improving hardware performance but also by increasing the classical difficulty, with different techniques contributing unequally to these phenomena. This work provides strong evidence that superior empirical performance of quantum hardware over all classical techniques is an achievable goal in quantum machine learning, albeit for an artificial problem. However, as with any application relying on observables, beating state-of-the-art simulation methods remains the primary challenge, as our matrix product state results here show.

paper.title: Toward Quantum Monte Carlo for Sovereign Debt Risk: A proof of concept
paper.abstract: We present a proof-of-concept pipeline that applies quantum amplitude estimation to the probability that a sovereign debt-to-GDP ratio exceeds a critical threshold at a given horizon. The pipeline combines a reduced two-factor Gaussian debt model linearized around its mean, quantum state preparation on a 32 x 32 grid, a weighted-adder circuit, an integer comparator, and Maximum Likelihood Amplitude Estimation (MLAE). On a noiseless statevector simulator with 500 shots per Grover power, the circuit estimate (a = 0.1152) agrees with the circuit's exact target amplitude (0.1153), and the observed estimation error is consistent with the amplitude-estimation scaling in the number of oracle calls. The model used here is deliberately simple: it admits a closed-form solution, so the contribution is a demonstration of the encoding and estimation workflow, not a practical advantage over classical methods. We discuss the conditions under which such a pipeline could become relevant and the obstacles that remain.

paper.title: Overcoming the Representational Limitations of Amplitude Encoding for Quantum Neural Networks
paper.abstract: Quantum Neural Networks (QNNs) offer a framework for learning functions from classical data, but their expressive power depends critically on how inputs are encoded into quantum states. Angle encoding can require resources that scale with the number of features, whereas amplitude encoding represents $d$ features using only $\mathcal{O}(\log_2 d)$ qubits. This compactness comes at a representational cost: normalization makes conventional amplitude encoding invariant to nonzero real rescaling of the input, up to an unobservable global phase. We show that this invariance induces an exact, architecture-independent restriction on the resulting hypothesis class. No downstream quantum circuit can distinguish inputs differing by nonzero real scaling. We develop a general condition under which deterministic preprocessing can remove this ambiguity and show that nonlinearity alone is insufficient. Based on this analysis, we introduce a fixed nonlinear feature map that provably distinguishes all real inputs under subsequent amplitude encoding, without adding trainable parameters and while retaining logarithmic qubit scaling. We evaluate the resulting QNN on three canonical classification benchmarks and a nonlinear synthetic dataset against conventional amplitude and angle encoding, as well as a classical neural network. Across these tasks, the proposed encoding consistently improves classification accuracy over both quantum encoding baselines by 21$-$44 %. Our results establish normalization-induced scale invariance as a concrete representational bottleneck of amplitude encoding and demonstrate that it can be removed while preserving a compact quantum representation, marking a step toward quantum models capable of capturing arbitrary relationships in classical data.

paper.title: Bounding Fidelity of Non-Stabilizer States from Local Pauli Measurements
paper.abstract: Nonstabilizerness, commonly referred to as magic, is essential for universal quantum computation. Yet, for pure $n$-qubit states this property is directly linked to the hardness of direct fidelity estimation. We propose a scheme to bound the fidelity on non-stabilizer states by choosing operators with low measurement overhead and using parallel local Pauli measurements to estimate compatible observables. We selectively measure operators that share a permutational symmetry without imposing any assumption on the physical system. This selection reduces the optimization to a linear program with only $O(n)$ variables for bounding fidelity. Our methods can be extended to bound nonlinear quantities like the purity via convex quadratic programs. For hypergraph states that can exhibit extensive nonstabilizerness, we demonstrate for up to $n=500$ qubits that our framework substantially reduces the measurement overhead under both local and global depolarizing noise. These results show that symmetry induced by measurement selection reduces both measurement and computational costs, enabling scalable characterization of magic resources in quantum computing and quantum networks.

paper.title: Quantum machine learning geospatial time-series by seasonal encoding
paper.abstract: Quantum data reuploading models can increase the expressive capacity of variational quantum models, but do not necessarily improve predictive performance. In the present work, we investigate this behavior for seasonal time series forecasting and show that data encoding determines how well temporal structures are represented as circuit depth increases. We develop a fidelity-based quantum geometric description in which repeated encodings contribute to an effective input generator, so that reuploading depth changes the quantum geometry through which approximately recurrent inputs are distinguished. We construct fixed and adaptive seasonal encodings that represent observation magnitude and seasonal phase in distinct Bloch-sphere coordinates. We evaluate these encodings for monthly precipitation derived from ERA5-Land, a global reanalysis dataset, from a representative semi-arid, drought-prone tropical region in East Africa, using a 14-month lag window and reuploading depths $L$= 1-6. We find that in ideal simulations, standard value-based encodings degrade markedly with depth, whereas adaptive seasonal encodings preserve temporal correlation, spectral structure, and forecasting accuracy. Noisy simulations show that this encoding hierarchy persists at shallow and intermediate depths, while larger depths are limited by circuit noise and optimization difficulty. The seasonal quantum models remain competitive with established classical forecasting methods (ARIMA, random forests, and LSTMs). These results identify structure-aware quantum data encoding as a general strategy for building deeper quantum reuploading models.

paper.title: FaultScope: A software package for fast error attribution in quantum error correction
paper.abstract: We introduce FaultScope, a classical simulator for quantum error correction circuits, implemented in Rust with a Python interface. FaultScope estimates logical error rates and their derivatives with respect to component error rates from the same sampled and decoded shots, without modifying or differentiating through the decoder. These derivatives enable error attribution to individual noisy components, helping identify noise hotspots for targeted noise reduction. FaultScope supports forward simulation of error propagation through circuits and direct sampling of detector and logical observable outcomes from detector error models. In our noiseless and noisy benchmarks, FaultScope has the lowest runtime among the tested simulators at every size. Computing all derivatives adds only 0.33--0.97\% to the runtime of logical error rate estimation across five repetition code sizes with 7--2047 error locations. FaultScope can be used to benchmark large-scale quantum error correction schemes and guide targeted noise reduction efficiently, thereby facilitating the design and optimization of fault-tolerant quantum computing architectures.

paper.title: High-efficiency photonic GHZ measurements with linear optics
paper.abstract: Probabilistic and destructive Bell-measurements, also known as fusions, constitute a fundamental primitive for photonic quantum technologies. These operations rely only on pairwise photonic interference, whereas the computational power of photonic quantum systems originates from many-body interference. Here, we introduce a family of high-efficiency linear-optical GHZ measurements based on four-mode interferometers and show that incorporating many-body interference into this ubiquitous primitive leads to more efficient entangling operations. For the four-photon case, the success probability is $9/32$, and adaptive variants ensure that unsuccessful events project onto useful stabilizer states. We further show that the approach naturally generalizes to larger GHZ measurements, yielding an exponentially higher success probability than previous linear-optical schemes. Finally, we demonstrate practical advantages for graph-state resource generation, entanglement distribution between remote spin-photon interfaces, and fusion-based quantum computing. Our results establish high-efficiency many-body measurements as a new primitive for scalable photonic quantum information processing.

paper.title: Real-time BP decoding of a high-rate QEC code
paper.abstract: We present a real-time FPGA decoder for a high-rate $[[512,174,8]]$ 3D product qLDPC code. We construct a circuit-level detector-error model for a compact syndrome-extraction schedule and propose a small parallel ensemble of row-wise serial min-sum decoders with cumulative memory. The decoder matches $\text{BP+OSD-CS}_\text{10}$ accuracy with one core and Relay-BP accuracy with three cores. The FPGA implementation meets the latency budget of neutral-atom and trapped-ion systems. An ASIC implementation would improve the latency, enabling real time decoding even for superconducting systems. At a physical error rate of $p=10^{-3}$, three FPGA devices decode 174 logical qubits with a logical error rate of $5\times10^{-7}$ and effective distance 6. For $p=10^{-4}$, and assuming the number of BP iterations is capped to 30, the decoder's average latency is $5.1\,$\textmu s and its worst-case latency is $97.9\,$\textmu s.

paper.title: Distilling Knowledge from Search: Decoder Model Factory for Quantum LDPC Codes
paper.abstract: We introduce GraphMP, a learning-based message-passing decoder for quantum low-density parity-check codes that transfers without fine-tuning across code families, code sizes, physical error rates, and noise models. GraphMP uses local message passing to keep computation scalable as the decoding graph grows. Guided by its predictions, beam search progressively refines candidate error patterns, trading additional decoding time for lower logical error rates. We develop the decoder model factory as a paradigm for training successive models on experience generated by earlier models during decoding. Model-guided search supplies verified trajectories for knowledge distillation, folding computation spent on decoding into reusable training data. Repeated collection and distillation improve the decoder across generations and adapt its strategy as the noise changes. These results motivate a coupled quantum--classical architecture with two interacting cycles: rapid decoding protects quantum information, while slower learning renews the models from operating experience. The long-term vision is a scalable decoder model factory that produces high-performance, low-latency decoders and continually adapts them to evolving quantum hardware.

paper.title: Loss-aware optimization of realistic GKP gid states
paper.abstract: Realistic preparation of Gottesman-Kitaev-Preskill (GKP) states, the prime candidates for quantum computation with bosonic systems, is inevitably burdened by photon loss. We show how taking this loss into account can lead to more robust quantum states, thereby diminishing its negative influence. Using GKP squeezing as an operational figure of merit, we formulate a loss-aware optimization procedure based on the ground state representation of GKP states. Numerical simulations for square, hexagonal, and asymmetric GKP states show that the optimal preparation generally requires a different initial grid spacing than that of the desired ideal code state. For symmetric and hexagonal lattices, the optimal parameters asymptotically follow the simple scaling relation. The optimized states exhibit better GKP squeezing and greater resilience to losses. These results provide a simple and experimentally relevant strategy for improving realistic photonic GKP state preparation in the presence of known photon loss.

paper.title: Time-Domain Multiplexing for Resource-Efficient Heralded GKP State Preparation
paper.abstract: Gottesman-Kitaev-Preskill (GKP) states are key resources for fault-tolerant photonic quantum computing, but their conditional preparation via Gaussian boson sampling involves a trade-off between source count and photon-number resolution. Distributing heralding photons across more measured modes reduces the resolution required per mode, yet increases the number of simultaneously operated squeezed sources in fully squeezed spatial architectures. Here, we show that time-domain multiplexing (TDM) can reduce these physical source requirements while preserving GKP state quality. Using an end-to-end differentiable Bargmann framework, we find that TDM circuits reusing one or two squeezed sources achieve fidelities comparable to fully squeezed spatial circuits across several configurations. Selected nine-mode configurations retain fidelities above 0.95 with one photon heralded in each measured mode, mitigating detector resolution demands without a proportional increase in source count. Loss-aware reoptimization further shows that, under the investigated spatial loss models, two-mode TDM maintains fidelities near 0.80 at 1.0 dB per channel, whereas the corresponding spatial benchmarks fall below 0.60. These results demonstrate that temporal reuse provides an effective architectural route for balancing source overhead, detection demands, and state preparation performance in the presence of optical loss.

paper.title: POST-MIMO: Partition-Oriented Semantic Transmission for MIMO Point Cloud Delivery
paper.abstract: Point clouds have become a fundamental data format for emerging three dimensional (3D) applications, while their wireless delivery remains challenging due to the large data volume and irregular geometric structure. Existing semantic point cloud transmission methods are mainly developed for single-input single-output systems, making them difficult to apply directly to multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) systems. To address this issue, we propose a partition-oriented semantic transmission framework for MIMO (POST-MIMO) point cloud delivery. POST-MIMO partitions the input point cloud into spatially coherent blocks and aligns them with parallel MIMO streams. Based on this block-aligned representation, the transmitter employs a hierarchical encoder to capture both intra-block local geometry and inter-block global dependency, while the auxiliary side information is transmitted jointly to assist reconstruction. At the receiver, a progressive decoder reconstructs the block geometry in a progressive manner and restores the final point cloud with block-aware adjustment. Experiments demonstrate improved reconstruction quality and lower computational resource consumption than representative reference schemes under the considered MIMO setting.

paper.title: Researcher-in-the-Loop Evolutionary Discovery of Entanglement-Assisted Quantum Code Families
paper.abstract: LLM-guided program evolution can produce mathematical constructions, but validity, generality, and reproducibility require distinct evidence. We develop a researcher-in-the-loop discovery pipeline that combines program evolution, exact evaluation, mathematical generalization, certified nonexistence checks, and formal proof checking. We apply it to entanglement-assisted quantum error-correcting codes (EAQECCs). Starting from tasks that did not specify a family formula, evolved programs produced finite qubit constructions whose structure researchers generalized to the family $[[n,1,n-1;n-q-1]]_q$ for prime powers $q\ge3$ at $n\ge2q+1$ and for $q=2$ at odd $n\ge5$. Lean checks the algebraic certificate underlying this family. Together with entanglement lifting, the family closes 54 gaps in archived EAQECC tables. The released evidence includes 115 verified code records, ten nonexistence results with checked DRAT proofs, family implementations, and preserved search programs for exact checks and seeded replay. In a controlled cohort of eight paired generation blocks, validation-selected iterative programs achieve success in 46.1% and 31.6% of held-out executions at unseen lengths $n=13,15$, compared with 19.5% and 3.1% for independently generated programs. In this setting, program evolution and researcher analysis turn finite computational discoveries into a proved family with independently checkable evidence.

paper.title: Privacy-Constrained Function Computation in Distributed Databases
paper.abstract: Consider distributed databases that contain both sensitive (private) and non-sensitive (public) attributes. A user seeks to compute a function of public attributes and side information by interacting with the databases and downloading their responses. In this paper, we study the trade-offs among download cost, information leakage about the private attributes, and distortion between the computed function and its reconstruction, referred to as the capacity region. Our main contributions are as follows. For a single database, we provide a complete characterization of the capacity region for general discrete sources and characterize the capacity region of two different setups for Gaussian sources when the computed function is defined as the sum of the public attribute and side information. For distributed databases, we establish inner and outer bounds on the capacity region of discrete sources and we characterize the capacity region when the databases and the side information are mutually independent. As a special instance, we study lossless function computation, and results analogous to the lossy case are obtained.

paper.title: Colloquium: Quantum information processing with ensembles of identical particles
paper.abstract: Identical particles underpin most quantum technologies, but the role of indistinguishability in these processes extends far beyond the symmetrization of many-particle states. This Colloquium presents a unified operational perspective on how particle identity, indistinguishability, exchange statistics, and many-particle interference can instead be harnessed as resources for quantum information processing. We first clarify the notions of entanglement and indistinguishability for identical particles, emphasizing their dependence on the accessible measurements and information. We then review how spatial overlap, multiparticle interference, and path identity enable the generation, extraction, protection, and distillation of coherence and entanglement. Their applications to quantum metrology and imaging, state discrimination, teleportation, entanglement swapping, and quantum cloning are examined. Finally, we discuss the thermodynamic role of indistinguishability, from the Gibbs paradox to quantum thermal machines and statistics-driven engines. Across these settings, indistinguishability emerges as a controllable, task-dependent resource whose benefits are determined by state preparation, exchange statistics, interference, and measurement constraints.

paper.title: Benchmarking One-Dimensional Quantum Lattice Boltzmann Methods on Quantum Hardware
paper.abstract: Classical computational fluid dynamics (CFD) methods encounter significant computational bottlenecks in large systems and at high Reynolds number flows due to the rapid increase in degrees of freedom, even on flagship supercomputers. As quantum computers emerge, the Quantum Lattice Boltzmann Method (QLBM) has been proposed as a quantum-native alternative for solving fluid dynamics problems. However, until recently, nearly all studies have relied on classical quantum simulators rather than real quantum hardware. This study presents a benchmark of a one-dimensional QLBM implementation executed on three different IBM Quantum hardware. We design and test a quantum circuit for the advection-diffusion equation using amplitude encoding, a Bhatnagar-Gross-Krook (BGK)-type collision operator, and a streaming step with periodic boundary conditions. Our numerical experiments evaluate transpiled two-qubit gate count, total circuit depth, runtime, and accuracy metrics including maximum absolute error ($L_\infty$ norm) and root-mean-square error (RMSE). We find that the present collision and streaming operators dominate the overall cost and become the primary scalability bottleneck on current hardware. To mitigate the prohibitive cost of full quantum state tomography on hardware-based benchmarking exercises, we introduce a sampler-based measurement strategy that reconstructs macroscopic density fields directly from computational-basis measurements. This approach substantially reduces measurement overhead while preserving the expected advection-diffusion dynamics on hardware. These results provide a quantitative assessment of QLBM performance in the noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) regime and identify the principal algorithmic and experimental limitations that must be addressed for QLBM to become viable for fluid dynamics.

paper.title: Learning Finite-Memory Binary Sources
paper.abstract: Estimating biased finite-memory sources from a single trajectory is a fundamental problem with practical impact, for example in estimating entropy for cryptography. We study order-$d$ binary sources whose conditional probabilities have bias at most $ε$, and establish *sharp* sample complexity bounds: relative accuracy $γ$ with confidence $1-δ$ needs $γ^{-2}\,(\tfrac12-ε)^{-d}\,(\log d+\log\tfrac1δ)$ samples up to constants depending on $ε$, with matching upper and lower bounds and no dependence on mixing time or spectral gap. The proof rests on a sharp bound on expected hitting times of the sliding-window (de Bruijn) chain, which stay of order $1/π(w)$ uniformly in $d$ exactly when $ε<\tfrac3{10}$, and on majorization of the window masses by those of independent biased coins. Applied to published entropy-source validations, the bounds show that their trace lengths may be underpowered: $10^6$ bits cannot resolve all transitions of an $8$-bit model to better than about $4.5\%$ relative error.
